extraction.name: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context
extraction.description: A large-scale dataset for object detection and segmentation containing 91 object types with 2.5 million labeled instances in 328k images. The dataset focuses on complex everyday scenes containing common objects in their natural context, with per-instance segmentations to aid in precise object localization.
extraction.creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár
extraction.citeAs: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár. Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context. arXiv:1405.0312v3 [cs.CV], 21 Feb 2015.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Images were collected from Flickr using pairwise combinations of object categories and scene/object category pairs to obtain non-iconic images. The dataset employed a novel pipeline using Amazon Mechanical Turk for annotation involving category labeling, instance spotting, and instance segmentation stages.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images were collected from Flickr by searching for pairwise combinations of object categories and scene/object category pairs. At most 5 photos were downloaded from a single photographer within a short time window.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Near-duplicate images were explicitly removed using detection algorithms, and images were grouped by photographer and date taken to minimize near-duplicates across dataset splits.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: An AMT filtering task was used to remove invalid or iconic images from candidate images. Workers were provided with examples of iconic and non-iconic images to guide the filtering process.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotation involved three stages: (1) category labeling using hierarchical approach where 8 workers labeled categories present in each image, (2) instance spotting where 8 workers placed crosses on all instances of each category (up to 10 instances), and (3) instance segmentation where workers segmented each object instance using a modified interface from OpenSurfaces project. Workers completed mandatory training tasks before segmenting instances. For images with more than 10 instances, remaining instances were marked as 'crowds' using a single segment.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) with custom user interfaces. Instance segmentation interface was modified from the OpenSurfaces project.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Category presence was determined by union of 8 workers' responses. A category was considered present if any worker indicated it; false positives were handled in subsequent stages. Analysis showed that 8 AMT workers achieved greater recall than individual expert workers. For instance segmentation, a verification step was implemented where 3-5 workers judged each segmentation, and segmentations requiring at least 4 of 5 favorable votes were kept.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 8 workers for category labeling, 8 workers for instance spotting, 1 worker for instance segmentation (with 3-5 workers for verification)
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Workers on Amazon's Mechanical Turk (AMT) were used for all crowdsourcing tasks. For the category labeling task, analysis showed that most workers had high precision, and workers who completed the most jobs also had the highest precision. Expert workers (co-authors of the paper) were also used for comparison and ground truth validation. Children ranging in ages from 4 to 8 were consulted to help compile the list of object categories by naming objects they see in indoor and outdoor environments.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset was split into two roughly equal parts. The first half (2014 release) contains 82,783 training, 40,504 validation, and 40,775 testing images. The cumulative 2015 release will contain a total of 165,482 train, 81,208 val, and 81,434 test images. Annotations for train and validation data are released, but not for test. The dataset will evolve and grow over time with up-to-date information available online.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset contains images of people as one of the object categories, with nearly 270k segmented people in the 2014 train+val data.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance object recognition and scene understanding, which has practical applications across computer vision. The paper notes that the selection of object categories considered their relevance to practical applications. The dataset enables research on detecting objects in natural contexts, which could impact various real-world applications including autonomous systems, accessibility technologies, and content understanding systems.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset focuses on 'thing' categories (objects with clear boundaries) and excludes 'stuff' categories (materials and objects with no clear boundaries like sky, street, grass). The dataset is limited to entry-level categories commonly used by humans rather than fine-grained categories. Some categories were removed due to ambiguity, confusion with other categories, or insufficient instances.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset currently only labels 'thing' categories and not 'stuff' categories, which could provide significant contextual information. The dataset is limited to entry-level categories and does not include fine-grained or object-part categories. Some object categories may have ambiguous presence in images, leading to inherent disagreement even among expert annotators. Training on non-iconic images may not always help if models are not rich enough to capture appearance variability.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for object detection and segmentation tasks in natural images. It can be used for training, validation, and testing of object recognition models. The dataset is particularly suited for learning complex models capable of precise 2D localization, contextual reasoning between objects, and detecting non-iconic views of objects. Baseline performance analysis is provided for bounding box and segmentation detection using Deformable Parts Model.

name.evidence: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context

description.evidence: We present a new dataset with the goal of advancing the state-of-the-art in object recognition by placing the question of object recognition in the context of the broader question of scene understanding. This is achieved by gathering images of complex everyday scenes containing common objects in their natural context. Objects are labeled using per-instance segmentations to aid in precise object localization. Our dataset contains photos of 91 objects types that would be easily recognizable by a 4 year old. With a total of 2.5 million labeled instances in 328k images

rai:dataCollection.evidence: We collected non-iconic images using two strategies. First as popularized by PASCAL VOC [2], we collected images from Flickr which tends to have fewer iconic images. Flickr contains photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords. Second, we did not search for object categories in isolation. A search for 'dog' will tend to return iconic images of large, centered dogs. However, if we searched for pairwise combinations of object categories, such as 'dog + car' we found many more non-iconic images. To create a large-scale dataset that accomplishes these three goals we employed a novel pipeline for gathering data with extensive use of Amazon Mechanical Turk.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: We collected non-iconic images using two strategies. First as popularized by PASCAL VOC [2], we collected images from Flickr which tends to have fewer iconic images. Flickr contains photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords. We downloaded at most 5 photos taken by a single photographer within a short time window.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: We collected non-iconic images using two strategies. First as popularized by PASCAL VOC [2], we collected images from Flickr which tends to have fewer iconic images. Flickr contains photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords. Second, we did not search for object categories in isolation... if we searched for pairwise combinations of object categories, such as 'dog + car' we found many more non-iconic images... We downloaded at most 5 photos taken by a single photographer within a short time window.

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: We took care to minimize the chance of near-duplicate images existing across splits by explicitly removing near duplicates (detected with [43]) and grouping images by photographer and date taken.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: To construct a high-quality set of non-iconic images, we first collected candidate images by searching for pairs of object categories, or pairs of object and scene categories. We then created an AMT filtering task that allowed users to remove invalid or iconic images from a grid of 128 candidates, Fig. 10. We found the choice of instructions to be crucial, and so provided users with examples of iconic and non-iconic images.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: The annotation pipeline is outlined in Fig. 3. For all crowdsourcing tasks we used workers on Amazon's Mechanical Turk (AMT)... The first task in annotating our dataset is determining which object categories are present in each image... To ensure high recall, 8 workers were asked to label each image... In the next stage all instances of the object categories in an image were labeled... Each image was labeled by 8 workers... Our final stage is the laborious task of segmenting each object instance... we required all workers to complete a training task for each object category... For images containing 10 object instances or fewer of a given category, every instance was individually segmented... After 10-15 instances of a category were segmented in an image, the remaining instances were marked as 'crowds' using a single (possibly multi-part) segment.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: For all crowdsourcing tasks we used workers on Amazon's Mechanical Turk (AMT). Our user interfaces are described in detail in the appendix... For this stage we modified the excellent user interface developed by Bell et al. [16] for image segmentation.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: To ensure high recall, 8 workers were asked to label each image. A category is considered present if any worker indicated the category; false positives are handled in subsequent stages... Fig. 4(a) shows that the union of 8 AMT workers, the same number as was used to collect our labels, achieved greater recall than any of the expert workers... While the training task filtered out most bad workers, we also performed an explicit verification step on each segmented instance to ensure good quality. Multiple workers (3 to 5) were asked to judge each segmentation and indicate whether it matched the instance well or not... At this point, any segmentation that doesn't receive at least 4 of 5 favorable votes is discarded

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: To ensure high recall, 8 workers were asked to label each image... Each image was labeled by 8 workers for a total of 10k worker hours... To minimize cost we only had a single worker segment each instance... Multiple workers (3 to 5) were asked to judge each segmentation

rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan.evidence: To accommodate a faster release schedule, we split the MS COCO dataset into two roughly equal parts. The first half of the dataset was released in 2014, the second half will be released in 2015. The 2014 release contains 82,783 training, 40,504 validation, and 40,775 testing images... The cumulative 2015 release will contain a total of 165,482 train, 81,208 val, and 81,434 test images... Following established protocol, annotations for train and validation data will be released, but not for test... MS COCO will evolve and grow over time; up to date information is available online.

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: There are nearly 270k segmented people and a total of 886k segmented object instances in the 2014 train+val data alone.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Since we are primarily interested in precise localization of object instances, we decided to only include 'thing' categories and not 'stuff.'... To enable the practical collection of a significant number of instances per category, we chose to limit our dataset to entry-level categories, i.e. category labels that are commonly used by humans when describing objects... We have limited the 2014 release to a subset of 80 categories. We did not collect segmentations for the following 11 categories: hat, shoe, eyeglasses (too many instances), mirror, window, door, street sign (ambiguous and difficult to label), plate, desk (due to confusion with bowl and dining table, respectively) and blender, hair brush (too few instances).

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: Since we are primarily interested in precise localization of object instances, we decided to only include 'thing' categories and not 'stuff.' However, since 'stuff' categories can provide significant contextual information, we believe the future labeling of 'stuff' categories would be beneficial... Object category presence is often ambiguous. Indeed as Fig. 4(a) indicates, even dedicated experts often disagree on object presence, e.g. due to inherent ambiguity in the image or disagreement about category definitions... Consistent with past observations [46], we find that including difficult (non-iconic) images during training may not always help. Such examples may act as noise and pollute the learned model if the model is not rich enough to capture such appearance variability.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We present a new dataset with the goal of advancing the state-of-the-art in object recognition by placing the question of object recognition in the context of the broader question of scene understanding... Our dataset is unique in its annotation of instance-level segmentation masks... we provide baseline performance analysis for bounding box and segmentation detection results using a Deformable Parts Model... MS COCO is designed for the detection and segmentation of objects occurring in their natural context... While MS COCO has fewer categories than ImageNet and SUN, it has more instances per category which we hypothesize will be useful for learning complex models capable of precise localization.
